points.claim: Q3, which this round built, was barely played. Only explorer-1-opus got into the museum. No run went down into the Royal Puzzle, and no run pushed the gold machine. The other two runs that reached the Great Door came before the earthquake, found the iron door rusted shut and turned back for good. In 776 explorer-1-opus found the Jewel Room door locked and the south stairs ending blindly, and nothing pointed back to pushing the machine into the Jewel Room in the present. The engine's reach figures agree: reach.places.never went from 8 to 52. That covers all 36 puzzle squares, cp_out, the five rooms of the years between, old_jewel_room and the water slide; reach.handlers.never went from 17 to 59.

evidence.quote: Museum Entrance ... To its left, however, is a cleft in the rock providing an exit from the museum.
it doesn't seem likely that you could climb back up
The door is locked, probably by the guards on their way out.
The stairs end blindly to the south.
The iron door is rusted shut and cannot be opened.
The iron door is rusted shut and cannot be opened.

points.recommendation: Give Q3's two gates a voice, in the way round 5 did for the repellent. Before the quake, the Great Door's rust, examined, should say the rock beside it is cracked and strained, so a visitor knows to come back. In 776, the locked stone door, or the guards' 'locked on their way out' line, should say the Jewel Room can only be reached from inside it. The present's gold machine, examined or pushed, should say it moves, for example scuffs on the floor or that it rolls a little at a touch. The hole at the puzzle entrance could say what lies below it (a ladder, a way out somewhere) so that 'can't climb back' is not the only thing it says.

points.claim: Goal-seeker reach. The sonnet goal-seeker (goal: get as far in as you can) did not get far. It killed the figure on the stroke after the waiting line (turn 17). It never found the Scenic Vista table, so it had no repellent, and it died in the grue lair (turn 57). It reached the rusted Great Door before the quake (turn 65) and stopped at the cliff ledge after four moves there (turns 93-98), before the man appeared. Its opus re-run went much further: the chest and the staff, the vial, the waybread and the secret door, the Timber Room, and the can from Room 8. Four deaths stood in its way: the fish on its first dive (turn 58), the altar, touched after looking at its image (turn 80), a grue in the lair after a 'look' spent the repellent's fifth move (turns 136-137), and the dark south of the stair after it left the respawned lamp behind (turn 140). The explorer re-run on opus also went much further than the sonnet explorer, which died in the grue lair at turn 130 without having touched the table. The opus explorer took the hood, got the vial, carried the repellent across to the key, pre-placed the torch through the table, entered the museum after the quake and pressed the button at 776. What stopped it: the aqueduct dead end (turns 114-139), the one-use repellent (172), the lamp lost while switched off (208-210), the locked Jewel Room in 776 (279), and a guard on its fourth death (325). Both opus runs ended in the Void, so their 'endings' are the losing kind.

evidence.quote: Oh, no! Dozens of lurking grues attack and devour you!
Perhaps what you seek is through there!
Room 8 ... A spray can is in the corner.
Good night, oh worthy adventurer!
Dozens of lurking grues attack and devour you!
From outside the door you hear the sounds of guards talking.
vaporizes you with a flick of his finger.

points.recommendation: No change to the odds. The blockers worth fixing are the ones filed below (P1, P3, P4, P6, P7, P8). Their common thread is lessons that are learned only by losing things, not lessons the world never teaches. Re-run the goal-seeker next round to see whether P3 and P7 move the sonnet runs past the lake.

points.claim: The Lake Shore's warning reads as a list of two things. It names 'your light first of all and your sword with it', so players left the light and the sword and went in with everything else. Explorer-1-opus lost the waybread (to mush) and the staff; goal-seeker-1-opus lost the staff and the vial. Both reports name this as the frustration.

evidence.quote: The waybread goes to mush in the water, and is gone.
The shock of entering the frigid water has made you drop all your possessions into the lake!

points.recommendation: Make the shore say everything: 'whatever you carry and cannot afford to lose to the bottom (everything in your hands, and your light first of all)'. Or name the waybread and the staff when they are carried. Leave the 'What you wear, it leaves you' clause as it is; that part works.

points.claim: The shore's told line 'a lit thing goes under here and comes up a dead one' teaches the wrong rule. Explorer-1-opus turned the lamp off to keep it and lost it anyway, and its report calls the warning misleading. The plunge line that followed has the switched-off lamp give 'a brief glow' as it goes under.

evidence.quote: a lit thing goes under here and comes up a dead one
The lamp is now off.
Your lamp goes under with the rest. There is a hiss, a brief glow in the water below you, and then not.

points.recommendation: Say that any lamp dies in the water, lit or not ('a lamp goes under here, lit or dark, and comes up a dead one'). Keep the 'shore is where it should be left' clause.

points.claim: The lamp's plunge line does not read the lamp's state. It gives 'a hiss, a brief glow' for a lamp turned off (turn 210), and again for a lamp the lake had already ruined, carried in a second time (turn 218).

evidence.quote: There is a hiss, a brief glow in the water below you, and then not.
it will not light again.
Your lamp goes under with the rest. There is a hiss, a brief glow in the water below you, and then not.

points.recommendation: Write three cases: lit (the hiss and the glow), off but whole (a hiss, no glow), and already ruined (it simply goes under with the rest).

points.claim: Round 5's waiting sequence on the ledge still says its first beat word for word for three moves running. Both opus runs got the 'lock being tried' line three times. Both reports call it a frustration ('I couldn't tell if anything was progressing'), and the repetition metric records it in both runs.

evidence.quote: the sound of a lock being tried, and tried again
the sound of a lock being tried, and tried again
the sound of a lock being tried, and tried again
the sound of a lock being tried, and tried again

points.recommendation: Key each beat to a single move, or give each stage two or three variants (lock tried; lid going back; somebody looking; coins), so that no wait repeats the one before it. The man's timing can stay the original's.

points.claim: The man at the cliff is still lost to the sonnet visitors. All three who reached the ledge without tying the chest left it, or quit, within two to five moves, before he showed himself. Each tried to talk to him in words the world does not read: 'call up to the person above' and 'call up to whoever is there' both got 'You can't see any such thing.' 'shout hello, can you help with the chest?' got 'That sentence isn't one I recognize.' 'say hello, can you help with the chest?' got the false not_here (friction 38). Both opus runs tied the chest at once and were hauled up.

evidence.quote: call up to the person above -> You can't see any such thing.
scramble down
call up to whoever is there -> You can't see any such thing.
That sentence isn't one I recognize.
You can't see any such thing.
down

points.recommendation: Read 'call up', 'call to <anyone>', 'call up to <anyone>' and 'shout <anything>' at the ledge as the shout that is already answered by stage. Have the stage-one chuckle say what he is waiting for, for example a remark about how heavy that chest looks from up here and whether there is a way to send it up. That gives the ledge a verb before a visitor's patience runs out. Leave his five-move timing alone.

points.claim: The repellent's terms are learned only by dying. Explorer-1-opus lost the can to the lake once, dived for it, and sprayed again: 'The repellent is all gone.' It then walked into the lair and died. Goal-seeker-1-opus spent the fifth move on a 'look' in the dark and died on the next. The 'much less pungent' warning did come, but as the last move began. The intent's 'a look on the way is one too many' works as a secret, but neither run knew the can held only one dose.

evidence.quote: The repellent is all gone.
You must have stumbled into an authentic grue lair!
That horrible smell is much less pungent now.
Dozens of lurking grues attack and devour you!

points.recommendation: Have `read can` or `examine can` give the label's small print: one application, a few minutes' protection. Keep the five moves exactly as they are.

points.claim: After the earthquake, the manhole leads to a dead end where the only way out is a fatal jump. The Key Room's draught and 'smell of open air' were not read as a warning. Explorer-1-opus went down, found the arch fallen and the hole out of reach, and spent 25 turns trying before it jumped to its death. It counted this among its worst moments ('Trapped').

evidence.quote: A thin draught comes up round its edges that was not there before the earth shook
it stops against the air: an arch has fallen since the earth shook
The hole is too far above your head.
This was not a very safe place to try jumping.

points.recommendation: This is faithful (the hint book's 'stuck'), so keep the trap but tell it at the brink. After the quake, opening or looking into the manhole should say the channel below goes nowhere now and that the drop is not one you climb back from.

points.claim: 'sit in machine' at the Technology Museum drew the black machine out of a three-way tie, and the engine warned 'drawn: the line read 3 ways that tied'. That cost a turn, even though only the gold machine has a seat. The brief's rule that a verb is offered only where something it applies to is in range would settle the tie.

evidence.quote: (the black machine) The black machine is a tangle of pipes and wires with no inside to it that a person would fit.

points.recommendation: Type the role of `sit in`/`enter`/`climb into` by a seat kind that only the gold machine composes, so that bare 'machine' resolves there. Leave the draw (friction 49) for verbs that all three machines answer.

points.claim: Small gaps in the named scenery and in throwing. The Aqueduct's description names 'the gap', and 'examine gap' gets not_here. 'throw key at balcony' says only 'Thrown.' and leaves the key at the visitor's feet, although round 5 refuses throws at things out of reach with a line. The Barren Area's 'vegetation' does not answer at the Cliff. 'put torch back on wall' at the Vista is not read.

evidence.quote: examine gap -> You can't see any such thing.
throw key at balcony -> Thrown.
There is a strange key here.
examine vegetation -> You can't see any such thing.
put torch back on wall -> You can't see any such thing.

points.recommendation: Add 'gap' and 'chasm' to the High Arch's and the Aqueduct's scenery. Refuse a throw at the distant balcony in round 5's voice ('far below, and the throw would fall short into the chasm'). Make 'vegetation' a word for the trees at the Cliff and for the far scenery at the Barren Area. Read 'put torch on wall' at the Vista as a drop, or answer it with a line.

points.claim: In the duel, one strike's two lines contradict each other. 'the hooded figure slips its sword between your ribs. You are hurt very badly.' is followed at once by the state line 'You have a few wounds, which do not seriously impair your strength.'

evidence.quote: You are hurt very badly. ... You have a few wounds, which do not seriously impair your strength.

points.recommendation: Remove the fixed 'You are hurt very badly' from that strike, or choose the strike's text by the wound it actually deals, as the stroke-side lines already are (round 3).

points.claim: The Vista's indicator change is told after the table's image, in the same turn. Goal-seeker-1-opus entered under 'III' and examined the table. It was shown the altar, view IV, and only then read 'changes to "IV"'. It waited one move and touched, and died at the altar. The trap itself is as intended; the order makes the image and the indicator disagree.

evidence.quote: An indicator above the table reads "III".
You see the interior of a huge temple ... The indicator above the table flickers briefly, then changes to "IV".
Sacrificial Altar ... slices you neatly across your abdomen.

points.recommendation: Tell the indicator's flicker before the image when the two fall in the same turn, so that the indicator and the image always agree when they are read.

points.claim: The hood trap is working as designed. Of the four duels fought to the figure's last point, two took the hood (the newcomer even struck once more without killing it) and two struck again on the very next command and killed it. Both of those reports wished afterwards that they had spared it, which is the trap doing its job.

evidence.quote: recoil in horror at the sight of your own face
remove hood
The hooded figure, fatally wounded, slumps to the ground.
The hooded figure, fatally wounded, slumps to the ground.

points.recommendation: Keep it, as round 5 did. No change.

points.claim: The fourth death ends the game without warning. Goal-seeker-1-opus woke from its third death, left the lamp at its feet on the lit stair, walked south into the dark and was eaten two moves later: game over. Explorer-1-opus's fourth death was a guard in 776. Goal-seeker-1-opus wished for a warning, or for the lamp to be put in its hands.

evidence.quote: There is a brass lantern here (providing light).
I have waited a long age for you, my friend, but perhaps it has been another that I have been seeking.
A particularly vicious-looking guard enters the room and sees you.

points.recommendation: Optional and in character: on the third visit, have the old man's line say his patience is nearly spent ('let me not wait long' made sharper). The lamp at the visitor's feet is the original's, so keep it.

points.claim: The casual player quit after 8 turns with nothing to do but walk. It took the stair, the junction, the stuck sword, the Cliff, the Land of Shadow and the ocean, met no figure, and found the dream's 'seek me' was never followed up.

evidence.quote: The sword is deeply imbedded in the rock. You can't budge it.
Cliff Base

points.recommendation: Low priority, since this is the original's opening. A cheap hook is the rope's twitch at the Cliff top, said on arriving there and not only on the ledge.

legibility.why: The runs that played deep read the world as intent.md has it. Explorer-1-opus named the trials as restraint and giving things up, the double under the hood, the thief with borrowed eyes, the lake that takes everything, and an examiner who keeps reviving you. Goal-seeker-1-opus turned the old man in the cell into a shopping list of the seven things. The newcomer got the core of Q1: you fight yourself and unhood it. The four short or stuck runs got only the frame: a Zork-like empire, a dream, an old man's final test, a hooded swordsman. Neither sonnet run that killed the figure understood the mercy until afterwards. No run said anything about Q3's changed past beyond explorer-1-opus's 777 plaque. One note on the harness's premise: both opus re-runs reached a losing 'ending' (the Void after a fourth death), and the newcomer was unsure whether unhooding was an ending. No run reached a winning end, which Q4 does not yet allow.

runs.understood: A Zork-like empire after a dream of a final test: dark passages, a stuck sword, a sunlit cliff, an ocean. Only geography, no goal.

A Zork-style final test set by a silver-haired old man. A cliff with an unseen watcher, a hooded swordsman, a freezing lake, a grue passage, a rusted door. The mercy hint was noticed only after killing the figure.

An old man tests whether you are worthy and gives your life back each time you die. The trials are about holding back and giving things up: your own face under the hood, a thief whose eyes are the old man's, a lake that takes everything, a time machine. Quiet and melancholy.
A Zork-like underground empire where a dream-old man says to seek him when worthy. A cliff, a lake, a land of shadow, a duel with a hooded figure whose mercy option was seen too late.

The old man waits at the bottom to judge worthiness. He wears the hood, cloak, amulet and ring and carries the book, staff and key, so the task is to collect those and earn the stair down. It is about earning things: a thief who keeps his word, a sailor's greeting, a hungry old man, a lake that takes all.
A dreamlike cave adventure about proving yourself worthy. The hooded figure you fight turns out to be you, and you spare it.
A Zork-tradition cavern after a dream-test: a sword in a rock, a land of shadows, a hooded figure, an underground sea, and a death handled by an old man in a cell.
A returning adventurer's final test at an endless stair, with a sword in a rock, a sunlit cliff oasis and an unseen figure toying with you from above.
